SUMMARY
The heroic fight of Ukrainians against the brutal aggression of the so-called Russian Federation requires enormous physical, intellectual, and emotional efforts from our people. Over the last three years, Ukrainian people have demonstrated outstanding resilience, although the atrocities of the war have had a significant negative impact on their physical and mental health. Veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, IDPs, and other groups affected by Russia's aggression need to have access to a reliable psychosocial rehabilitation service in their communities.
The GURT project Psychosocial Self-Assistance to Restore and Support Ukraine's Communities aimed at restoring life potential and opening possibilities for social empowerment for at least 3000 victims of the war in Ukraine by implementing a model of self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation and organizing the work of 10 partner NGOs that will provide immediate psychosocial rehabilitation and support for victims of the war.
By the end of the project, more than 5100 people became beneficiaries of the project, and 3345 representatives of veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs completed the full cycle of self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation. GURT has carefully selected, trained, and closely managed 10 partner NGOs that provided immediate psychosocial rehabilitation and support to people affected by Russia's aggression in 11 municipal communities, including Kyiv, Berdychiv, Dnipro, Ivano-Frankivsk, Khmelnytsky, Lutsk, Lviv, Poltava, Rivne, Vinnytsia, and Zhytomyr.
Almost 75% of project beneficiaries confirmed a significant improvement in their mental health conditions after the full cycle of group psychosocial rehabilitation, and 83% of project beneficiaries reported that their communication and cooperation with other community members became easier.
KEY ACTIVITIES
Activity 1.1 Infrastructure for self-help rehabilitation of NGO partners in 10 oblasts of Ukraine financially supported by the project.
During the project implementation, GURT has carefully selected, trained, and closely managed 10 partner NGOs that provided immediate psychosocial rehabilitation and support to people affected by Russia's aggression in 11 municipal communities, including Kyiv, Berdychiv, Dnipro, IvanoFrankivsk, Khmelnytsky, Lutsk, Lviv, Poltava, Rivne, Vinnytsia, and Zhytomyr.
GURT has designed software to monitor attendance at self-help group meetings and ensure project beneficiaries' confidentiality.
Partner NGOs used project funds to set up a community-based self-help group psychosocial support center, investing in creating a safe and comfortable space for self-help group meetings and promoting their services among veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs.
Activity 1.2 Capacity of at least 100 self-help group facilitators and practitioners built.
More than 100 self-help group facilitators were trained during the project implementation period. Gurt has combined online and face-to-face training formats to offer flexible capacity-building opportunities for potential self-help group facilitators nominated by partner NGOs.
Facilitators have been trained to run self-help group sessions in a format that allowed all participants to share their feelings and emotions in a non-violent and non-confrontational way. The facilitator provided a safe and confidential space where people who suffered from the war could openly discuss their individual situations and receive mutual emotional support from other members of a self-help group. To become a facilitator, an individual had to have personal experience of going through self-help group rehabilitation, demonstrate adequate social skills, and obtain a certificate of a self-help group facilitator. GURT provided this certification program that included intensive training and supervision of facilitators performance.
Experienced master trainers designed and conducted interactive trainings covering the theory and practice of self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation methodology. Face-to-face workshops in Kyiv were accompanied by online consulting and mentorship between training sessions. As a result, all partner NGOs were well-equipped with professional facilitators to ensure high-quality services in their communities.
Supervision intervention in March-April 2024 showed that 58% of self-help group facilitators are in a stable psychological state, and 42% of facilitators are at risk of emotional burnout. The long-term impact on the psyche of the facilitators in the conditions of war led to negative consequences regarding the deterioration of their professional health in terms of physical and psychological components. In contrast, social and spiritual health indicators were determined at an average level, determining purposefulness and motivation. Also, it was found that the dominant coping strategy in stressful situations is the focus on emotions, which determined the priority of manifestations of negative emotions, reduced levels of adaptation, and vitality. These together are signs of professional (emotional) burnout and the need to provide psychological support measures. GURTs experts offered online mentorship support and supervision for self-help group facilitators to prevent burnout and inspire their work.
Activity 2.1 Self-help group psycho-social rehabilitation model designed.
GURT has promoted the methodology of self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation at the community level in Ukraine since 2008. In 2014, the organization started to adapt the methodology to help the growing number of Ukrainians suffering from Russia's aggression.
Self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation is a peer-to-peer process that gives individuals power over their own rehabilitation. Instead of being passive patients in traditional therapy, self-help group members play an active role during the rehabilitation process, which makes the results more sustainable.
Self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation is a community-based rehabilitation that does not require the involvement of medical professionals. However, there are specific criteria that any individual should meet before joining a self-help group, including being able to participate in social activities safely. If a particular person needs professional psychological care, this person is referred to a certified psychologist.
The project beneficiaries have been veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs. NGO partners that provided self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation in their communities informed potential self-help group members about an opportunity to get support and improve their emotional and psychological state. All interested people in need have been interviewed by a trained self-help group facilitator, who checked if a particular person met eligibility criteria or referred a person to a different support institution.
All NGO partners had a list of reliable references in their communities that provided different types of support if a particular persons need couldn't be met through a self-help group. Facilitators were trained to run self-help group sessions in a format that allowed all participants to share their feelings and emotions in a non-violent and non-confrontational way.
The facilitator provided a safe and confidential space where people who suffered from the war could openly discuss their individual situations and receive mutual emotional support from other members of a self-help group. To become a facilitator, an individual had to have a personal experience of going through self-help group rehabilitation, demonstrate adequate social skills, and obtain a certificate of a self-help group facilitator. GURT provided this certification program that included intensive training and supervision of facilitators performance.
A self-help group session is basically a facilitated conversation among participants who share a common challenge or issue. It should be conducted in a safe and isolated space where self-help group members are not disturbed by any strangers. A standard self-help group session consisted of 4 parts: welcoming, core conversation, conclusions, and informal communication with tea and coffee.
Project experts developed an effective model of psychosocial rehabilitation for three specific beneficiaries: veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs. It is an ongoing action research initiative based on real-time data collection and monitoring results undertaken in close cooperation with partner NGOs. For now, there is a developed and accumulated set of training materials on how to establish a community-based self-help group psychosocial support center and how to train self-help group facilitators who work with veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs.
Activity 2.2 Community of practice of self-help group facilitators formed
More than 100 self-help group facilitators were trained during the project implementation period. These facilitators formed a community of practice that regularly met for face-to-face and online best practice sharing and learning exchange events.
A community of practice serves as a platform for facilitators to gain new knowledge and skills and as a virtual self-help group to deal with professional (emotional) burnout.
All facilitators have access to the knowledge base through Google Drive. They can review training materials, webinar recordings, and study sessions that cover specific topics on providing psychosocial support for veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs.
Two networking conferences were organized in the frame of the project: in November 2022 in Lviv and in July 2023 in Kyiv https://gurt.org.ua/gurt/selfhelp/events/#gsc.tab=0.
Following the same self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation model, each partner NGO had specific approaches and techniques. Sharing unique experiences made the joint work more prosperous and more productive.
IMPACT ASSESSMENT
In May-June 2024, GURT conducted an impact assessment among 3345 project beneficiaries, representatives of veterans, family members of Ukrainian defenders, and IDPs who completed the full cycle of self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation. The assessors have collected 385 responses, exceeding 10% of the respondents who received the questionnaire. Regarding the audience that participated in the online survey, on could notice that 42% were family members of Ukrainian defenders, 40.5% - IDPs, and 1.6% comprised veterans. Almost 16% declared a different status of people affected by the war. The sample shows its versatility and corresponds to the general results of the project regarding the involvement of different categories according to the GURTs monitoring software.
The survey aimed to determine changes in self-help group attendants' behavior related to community life participation. Based on the impact assessment results, it could be confirmed that the project significantly contributed to the resilience of Ukrainian communities, where our partner NGOs provided self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation support for people affected by the war.
Regarding changes in communication and interaction with other people in the community, it became evident that 83.4% of respondents noted that it became easier for them to communicate and interact with other people, 15.6% did not notice any changes, and only 1% of respondents testified that after attending a self-help group, it became more difficult for them to communicate in the community. This can be related to many factors, such as the person realizing that the surrounding people did not suit them and the previous circle of communication, the person's bubble, ceased to satisfy their needs due to internal growth, transformation, or awareness of traumatic relationships and abusive relationships, etc.
The question about participation in various community activities demonstrated the involvement of self-help group members in the life of the communities. As the answers showed, most people directed their activities to public events, volunteer projects, and joint actions with neighbors (interaction with the micro-society), although attending meetings with local authorities less often. Only 10% of people noted that they did not participate in any proposed activities. However, the fact that people become members of self-help groups is an integral indicator of interaction with society and the desire to participate in society in one way or another.
More than half of the respondents fully agreed that as a result of self-help group socio-psychological rehabilitation, they built new connections in the community and revealed the potential to make new social bridges and support them. They became more connected to the community, feeling greater involvement and personal interest. This could be assumed as a natural healing process due to human connections. It indicated a persons understanding of their societal role, necessity, and significance. The survey's final question aimed at determining the respondents' understanding of the fact that by attending self-help groups, they could model chains of mutual support and help each other and then transfer obtained skills to the macro-society of the communities in which they lived. This possibility was seen by almost 80% of the respondents, which indicated that they have sufficiently restored or developed the necessary communication and interaction skills for a more active and productive life in their communities, which was a critical contribution to community resilience during the war.
OUTLOOK
The project collected comprehensive evidence of the self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation model's effectiveness in restoring the lives of people affected by the war and contributing to community resilience. Continuing Russia's aggression requires scaling up the efforts to provide accessible community-based rehabilitation for Ukrainians. Most Ukrainians affected by Russia`s aggression experienced different forms of psychological disorder, including PTSD and depression. According to the World Health Organization, it is estimated that at least 9.6 million Ukrainians may be experiencing mental health problems because of the conflict.
GURT developed and established a network of 25 nonprofits across the country capable of providing self-help group psychosocial rehabilitation and support services to demobilized veterans, family members of active, killed-in-action, prisoners of war, or missing Ukrainian defenders, and internally displaced people. This network in in the need of continued consistent financial support to provide vital services in their communities.
Continuity is a significant factor in psychosocial rehabilitation effectiveness. From January 2023 to March 2024, 5119 people affected by Russia's aggression registered to get psychosocial rehabilitation and support services from the project partner NGOs. Its 171% more direct beneficiaries than what was initially planned in the project. Today, the CSO cannot provide necessary services to many people who have started but have not yet finished the rehabilitation process because of the lack of financial resources. Moreover, the CSO continues to receive many new registrations of people interested in getting psychosocial support, disregarding the formal expiration of the project's first phase.
GURT is also receiving many requests from veteran NGOs and networks, such as Caritas, Military Capelan Service, Union of People with Disabilities, and Association of IDPs, who are interested in replicating the methodology of self-help psychosocial rehabilitation.
GURT required resources to disseminate the successful psychosocial rehabilitation model across the country. The CSO plans to do this by training capable NGOs and their networks and running information campaigns to promote this accessible community-based rehabilitation for people affected by Russia's aggression. Many success stories of individuals who underwent rehabilitation and our partner NGOs are available at GURTs portal https://gurt.org.ua/gurt/selfhelp/results/#gsc.tab=0.
The dedicated program website is vital for a more effective information campaign to attract new beneficiaries, ensure knowledge transfer, further model replication, and quality assurance.
